## What this is

A Go library implementing the **circuit breaker pattern** for fault tolerance
and graceful degradation in distributed systems. Three states (`CLOSED`,
`OPEN`, `HALF_OPEN`), configurable failure thresholds and timeouts,
automatic recovery, state-change callbacks, and metrics.

It is the canonical text-book circuit breaker — well-scoped, well-tested,
well-documented. The local snapshot has 4 commits ending with a documentation
update; the implementation predates that.

## What it was good at

- **High performance** — claimed `<1µs` state checks via minimal-overhead
  fast path. Suitable for in-line use on every outbound request.
- **Functional options** — clean Go-idiomatic configuration API.
- **State-change callbacks** — clean observability hook for metrics/UI
  integrations.
- **Test coverage** — the commit history shows a dedicated test-suite
  commit (`492d16d Add comprehensive test suite for circuit breaker`)
  fixing deadlocks and failures (`86dd9dc Fix circuit-breaker test
  deadlocks and failures`). The tests are part of the artifact, not a
  post-hoc add-on.

The architecture is the part worth re-reading. `ARCHITECTURE.md` lays it
out; the implementation lives in `pkg/`. The state-machine semantics (the
transitions, the failure counting window, the half-open trial policy) are
the load-bearing design decisions.

## Why we moved on

The circuit breaker pattern is now considered table-stakes; most language
ecosystems have at least one well-maintained library (Hystrix-style for
JVM, sony/gobreaker for Go, etc.). Beyond that, the architecture question
collapsed: in 2024+ distributed systems, sidecar-based service meshes
(Istio, Linkerd, Envoy) handle bulkheading and circuit breaking at the
infrastructure layer, not in application code. Writing a new application-
layer circuit breaker offered diminishing returns.

This archive preserves the moment when the pattern was still something
you wrote yourself — before it moved into infrastructure.

## How to use this archive

If you want to use the library:

```bash
go test ./...          # run the tests in tests/
go run examples/...    # runnable examples
```

The README has a Quick Start that imports `circuit-breaker` as a module;
replace `yourusername` with `SuperInstance` if you fork it.

If you want to study the pattern:

- `README.md` for the API and quick start.
- `ARCHITECTURE.md` for the state machine and design rationale.
- `pkg/` for the implementation.
- `tests/` for the test suite — particularly the failure-injection tests
  that verify the state transitions under load.

## How to get the big pieces

No model weights, no datasets, no vendored binaries. To use the library you
only need a Go toolchain (the `go.mod` declares `go 1.x`). All dependencies
are resolved through standard Go modules.

## Salvageable mechanisms

- **State machine as the implementation's spine** — `CLOSED → OPEN →
  HALF_OPEN → CLOSED` with explicit transition rules. A generalizable
  shape for any "fail-open / fail-closed" component.
- **Counter window vs. rolling window** — implementation choices here
  (sliding time window, exponential decay, fixed bucket) have outsized
  impact on the steady-state behavior. Worth reading the implementation
  choices in `pkg/`.
- **State-change callback pattern** — a clean observability seam that
  integrates with Prometheus / OpenTelemetry without coupling. Useful
  even in non-circuit-breaker state machines.
